metadata.title: Assessing the Linguistic Creativity Domain of Last-Year Compulsory Secondary School Students

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study collected primary paper-based data from 454 Spanish students in eight high school centers during the 2021–2022 academic year, rather than using an international large-scale assessment microdata file. Because the analysis is based on a convenience sample of schools/students in Spain and the methodology does not mention any complex survey design, sampling weights, or replicate-weight procedures, no ILSA-style student weights (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) are applied. The reported scoring procedures for the three creativity tasks (semantic distance for naming unrelated words, rubric-based metaphor scoring with interrater reliability, and PIC-J fluency/flexibility/originality scoring) are treated as direct test scores, not as PV-based achievement estimates. Consequently, the weighting guidance relevant to ILSA PV/scaling is not applicable here; the results reflect unweighted descriptive and inferential statistics on the analytic sample.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the dependent variables are creativity-task scores derived from paper-based tasks (semantic distance percentage, metaphor categories/points, and PIC-J fluency/flexibility/originality), not cognitive achievement scales that are typically PV-based in ILSA programs. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data handling procedure (e.g., exclusion rules or imputation), so the missing-data strategy cannot be verified from the provided text. This is a reporting gap for transparency about how incomplete task responses were treated.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were 454 Spanish students in their last year of compulsory secondary education (fourth grade; ages 14–17, mean 15.3) recruited from eight Spanish high school centers (rural and urban areas in eastern Spain). The study reports that all students, teachers, and legal tutors agreed to participate and that informed consent/ethics documentation was obtained. The methodology does not specify additional inclusion/exclusion filters beyond participation and the task administration protocol; it also does not report any explicit rule for handling incomplete or invalid responses beyond task-specific scoring steps (e.g., discarding inappropriate metaphor answers and discarding non-noun syntactic categories for the naming task).

main_findings.dataset_used: ILSA assessment context not specified in extraction (heuristic migration)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ILSA assessment context not specified in extraction (heuristic migration) the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This study used a Spanish convenience sample (N=454) of last-year compulsory secondary students (fourth grade; ages 14–17) to assess linguistic creativity through three paper-based tasks: naming unrelated words (semantic distance percentage), metaphor generation (novel/conventional/literal scoring), and the alternate uses task (PIC-J fluency, flexibility, originality). The analysis did not train or evaluate any machine-learning model; instead, it reports descriptive statistics, gender-group comparisons (t-test/Mann–Whitney U), and Pearson correlations among task scores. Key results include moderate performance on naming unrelated words (M=79.3, SD=4.4) and alternate uses total (M=33.6, SD=16.9), while metaphor generation performance was lower (M=11.2, SD=4.6) with only 7% novel metaphors reported in the discussion. Gender differences were found for metaphor generation (p=0.01, g=0.11) and alternate uses total (p<0.001, g=0.17), but not for naming unrelated words (p=0.34). Correlations were significant between metaphor generation and naming unrelated words (p=0.035) and between metaphor generation and alternate uses (p=0.001), while naming unrelated words and alternate uses were not significantly correlated (p=0.030). Limitations include non-representativeness of the sample and lack of explicit missing-data handling documentation. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an empirical, non-ML study: the methodology uses SPSS-based descriptive statistics, group tests, and Pearson correlations rather than predictive modeling. As a result, fields related to machine-learning techniques, PV handling, and ML-based target prediction are not applicable or cannot be populated with meaningful values. The paper also does not report a missing-data handling protocol, which is why missing_data_handling is set to not_reported.
